Self-repair — can it fix its own bugs?

Each task gets up to 5 attempts; after a failure the model is handed its own code plus the compiler/test output. Cells show one-shot passes, then +n fixed using the feedback and ✗n still broken after 5 rounds. gen time is the whole suite — every round of every task, failed attempts included — and counts model generation only, not local compiling and testing. waste = tokens spent on tasks that needed more than one round. C = 19 tasks, Python and Bash = 11 each.

The referee is excluded here: it's a cloud model, so the harness couldn't drive it. Its C figures (18/19 one-shot) are self-reported and have no token or timing data.

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, situated in the vibrant intellectual hub of Cambridge, Massachusetts, stands not merely as an educational institution but as a colossal engine of innovation that has fundamentally reshaped the trajectory of artificial intelligence, serving as the crucible where theoretical mathematics, computational engineering, and cognitive science converge to produce breakthroughs that define the modern digital age. From its earliest days as a polytechnic institute focused on practical application, MIT cultivated a culture of "mens et manus," or mind and hand, which proved to be the perfect philosophical foundation for the development of AI, a field that requires both abstract algorithmic thinking and tangible hardware implementation, thereby creating a unique ecosystem where researchers are encouraged to build, test, and iterate rapidly, a methodology that has allowed MIT to consistently lead the global charge in defining what machines can think, learn, and perceive. The historical roots of this influence are deeply embedded in the post-World War II era, when the university became a central node in the nascent field of cybernetics and early computing, with figures like Norbert Wiener and later Marvin Minsky laying the groundwork for understanding intelligence as a computational process, a perspective that shifted the paradigm from biological mimicry to logical simulation and set the stage for the symbolic AI revolution of the 1960s and 1970s. Minsky’s establishment of the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory at MIT was a watershed moment, creating a dedicated space where the limitations of early logic-based systems were rigorously tested and where the concept of "common sense" reasoning began to be formalized, influencing generations of researchers who would go on to populate Silicon Valley and other tech hubs, effectively exporting MIT’s intellectual capital to the broader world. As the field evolved from symbolic logic to connectionism and neural networks, MIT remained at the forefront, particularly through the work of researchers like John Hopfield, whose development of the Hopfield network provided a crucial bridge between physics and neuroscience, offering a mathematical framework for associative memory that would later inform the architecture of modern deep learning models. This interdisciplinary approach is a hallmark of MIT’s AI research, where the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), one of the largest and most prominent research centers in the world, operates not as a siloed department but as a collaborative nexus that integrates electrical engineering, mechanical engineering, linguistics, and even the arts, recognizing that true intelligence is multifaceted and cannot be understood through a single disciplinary lens. In the realm of computer vision, MIT researchers have been instrumental in developing algorithms that allow machines to interpret visual data with unprecedented accuracy, moving beyond simple pattern recognition to semantic understanding, enabling technologies such as autonomous vehicles, medical imaging diagnostics, and real-time video analysis, all of which rely on the foundational work done in MIT’s labs on convolutional neural networks and generative adversarial networks. The influence of MIT extends deeply into natural language processing, where the university’s contributions to machine translation, sentiment analysis, and conversational AI have been pivotal, with researchers developing models that can understand context, nuance, and ambiguity in human language, a challenge that has long plagued AI systems and one that MIT’s work on transformer architectures and attention mechanisms has helped to mitigate. Furthermore, MIT has been a leader in the field of reinforcement learning, where agents learn optimal behaviors through trial and error, a technique that has powered advancements in robotics, game playing, and resource management, with MIT researchers developing novel algorithms that improve sample efficiency and stability, making these powerful techniques more accessible and applicable to real-world problems. The university’s commitment to open science and collaboration is evident in its release of numerous open-source tools and datasets, such as the ImageNet dataset contributions and various machine learning libraries, which have democratized access to AI research and accelerated progress globally by allowing researchers everywhere to build upon MIT’s foundational work. Beyond pure technical innovation, MIT has played a critical role in addressing the ethical and societal implications of AI, establishing initiatives like the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing, which was created with a $1 billion gift to integrate AI and data science across all disciplines, ensuring that future leaders in every field, from biology to economics to law, are equipped with the computational literacy necessary to navigate an AI-driven world. This holistic approach recognizes that AI is not just a technical challenge but a social one, and MIT’s research into fairness, accountability, and transparency in AI systems has been crucial in highlighting biases in algorithms and developing methods to mitigate them, influencing policy discussions and industry standards worldwide. The impact of MIT on robotics is equally profound, with the university’s work on soft robotics, swarm intelligence, and human-robot interaction pushing the boundaries of what machines can physically do, creating robots that can navigate complex environments, collaborate with humans, and perform delicate tasks, applications that range from disaster response to personalized healthcare. In the domain of healthcare, MIT’s AI research has led to the development of diagnostic tools that can detect diseases earlier and more accurately than human experts, using deep learning to analyze medical images and genomic data, potentially saving countless lives by enabling personalized medicine and predictive analytics. The university’s influence also extends to the hardware side of AI, with researchers developing specialized chips and architectures that optimize the performance of neural networks, addressing the growing energy and computational demands of large-scale AI models, a critical consideration as the environmental impact of computing becomes a major concern. MIT’s alumni network, often referred to as the "MIT Mafia" in tech circles, includes countless founders and executives of leading AI companies, who carry the institute’s ethos of rigorous inquiry and practical application into the private sector, driving commercial innovation and bringing academic breakthroughs to market. The collaborative spirit at MIT is further exemplified by its partnerships with industry giants and government agencies, creating a feedback loop where real-world problems inform academic research and academic discoveries are rapidly deployed to solve those problems, a model that has proven highly effective in maintaining MIT’s position at the cutting edge of AI. As we look to the future, MIT continues to pioneer research in areas such as explainable AI, where the goal is to make black-box models transparent and understandable, a necessity for building trust in AI systems, and in neuromorphic computing, which seeks to mimic the brain’s energy-efficient processing capabilities, potentially revolutionizing how we think about computation. The institute’s emphasis on education ensures that these advancements are not just confined to the lab but are taught to the next generation of scientists and engineers, with curricula that blend theoretical depth with hands-on experience, producing graduates who are not only technically proficient but also ethically aware and socially responsible. MIT’s role in shaping the global AI landscape is undeniable, serving as a beacon of innovation that inspires and guides the direction of the field, from the fundamental mathematics of learning to the practical applications that touch every aspect of modern life. The university’s ability to adapt and evolve, embracing new paradigms while maintaining its core values of excellence and integrity, ensures that it will remain a dominant force in AI research for decades to come, continuing to push the boundaries of what is possible and challenging us to think more deeply about the relationship between humans and machines. In essence, MIT’s influence on AI is not just about the specific algorithms or technologies it has produced, but about the culture of inquiry, collaboration, and responsibility it has fostered, creating a legacy that extends far beyond the campus and into the very fabric of our technological society, reminding us that the true power of AI lies not in its ability to replace human intelligence, but in its potential to augment and enhance it, a vision that MIT has championed from the beginning and continues to pursue with unwavering dedication.

#include <ctype.h>

int count_words(const char *s) {
    int count = 0;
    int in_word = 0;

    if (s == NULL) {
        return 0;
    }

    while (*s != '\0') {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)*s)) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else {
            if (!in_word) {
                count++;
                in_word = 1;
            }
        }
        s++;
    }

    return count;
}

            // So '+' is not part of well-formed input. We should not expect it.

        // Check if we have digits

            // Invalid character for a number start. Stop.

        }

        long long val = 0;
        int overflow = 0;
        
        while (*p >= '0' && *p <= '9') {
            int digit = *p - '0';
            if (val > (LLONG_MAX - digit) / 10) {
                overflow = 1;
            }
            val = val * 10 + digit;
            p++;
        }

        if (overflow) {
            // Handle overflow? Spec says well-formed, so maybe no overflow.
            // But if it happens, we might clamp or stop.
            // Let's just store what we can or stop.
            // For now, let's just use the value modulo or clamp.
            // Actually, if input is well-formed integers, they should fit in int?

            // Let's clamp or just cast.
            if (sign == -1) {
                if (val > (long long)INT_MAX + 1) {

                }
            } else {

                    val = INT_MAX;
                }
            }
        }

        int result = (int)(sign * val);
        out[count] = result;
        count++;

        // After digits, expect comma or end of string
        if (*p == ',') {
            p++;
            // If next char is not valid start of number and not end, but spec says well-formed,
            // so after comma should be another number or end.
            // If p points to '\0' after comma, loop will end.
            // But if there's a trailing comma, *p == '\0', loop condition *p != '\0' fails? 
            // No, we check *p != '\0' at start of loop. But we already incremented p past comma.
            // If *p is '\0', loop ends. Good.
        } else if (*p == '\0') {
            break;
        } else {

}

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    const char *p = pat;
    const char *s = str;
    const char *star_p = NULL;
    const char *star_s = NULL;

    while (*s) {
        if (*p == '*') {
            star_p = p;
            star_s = s;
            p++;
        } else if (*p == '?' || *p == *s) {
            p++;
            s++;
        } else if (star_p) {
            p = star_p + 1;
            star_s++;
            s = star_s;
        } else {
            return 0;
        }
    }

    while (*p == '*') {
        p++;
    }

    return *p == '\0' ? 1 : 0;
}

    r->count++;

}

#include <stddef.h>

typedef struct {
    int data[8];
    int head;
    int count;
} Ring;

static inline void ring_init(Ring *r) {
    r->head = 0;
    r->count = 0;
}

static inline int ring_push(Ring *r, int v) {
    if (r->count == 8) {
        return -1;              // buffer full
    }
    int tail = (r->head + r->count) % 8;
    r->data[tail] = v;
    r->count++;
    return 0;
}

static inline int ring_pop(Ring *r, int *out) {
    if (r->count == 0) {
        return -1;              // buffer empty
    }
    *out = r->data[r->head];
    r->head = (r->head + 1) % 8;
    r->count--;
    return 0;
}

/* glob_match.c
 * Shell‑style pattern matching: '*' = any sequence (including empty),
 * '?' = any single character, other characters match literally.
 * Returns 1 on match, 0 otherwise.
 * Conforms to C11.
 */

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str)
{
    const char *p = pat;   /* pattern pointer */
    const char *s = str;   /* string pointer */
    const char *star = NULL;   /* last '*' in pattern */
    const char *ss   = NULL;   /* position in string after last '*'-matched chars */

    while (*s) {
        if (*p == '*') {
            /* remember position of '*', advance pattern */
            star = p++;
            ss = s;
        } else if (*p == '?' || *p == *s) {
            /* single‑character match */
            p++;
            s++;
        } else if (star) {
            /* mismatch after a previous '*': backtrack */
            p = star + 1;   /* pattern resumes after '*' */
            s = ++ss;       /* consume one more character from string */
        } else {
            return 0;       /* no '*' to backtrack to and characters differ */
        }
    }

    /* Consume trailing '*' in pattern */
    while (*p == '*')
        ++p;

    return (*p == '\0');
}

- **Default maximum `rsize`/`wsize` raised to 1 MiB** – In RHEL 10 the client and server negotiate a maximum read/write size of 1 048 576 bytes (up from previous limits). - **FS‑Cache client‑side caching for NFS** – The new FS‑Cache integration (via the `cachefiles` backend and `cachefilesd` daemon) lets NFS clients cache file data locally on ext3/ext4/XFS. This can dramatically cut network traffic and server load for read‑heavy workloads, though it may add a small local‑cache overhead on the client.

- **Bug fix: IPv6 address handling in `nfs://` URLs (ReaR)** – ReaR now correctly parses IPv6 literals enclosed in `[…]` for `nfs://` (and `sshfs://`) schemes. The previous mis‑interpretation caused backup/restore jobs that used NFS over IPv6 to abort. The fix restores reliable NFS client operation in automated backup scenarios.

- **Mount‑option alias `vers` added (compatibility)** – The `vers` option is now accepted as a synonym for `nfsvers`. While not a performance change, it smooths migration of scripts and tools that rely on the older name.

The institute’s commitment to open science and data sharing, as seen in initiatives such as the MIT OpenCourseWare and the MIT AI Ethics and Governance Initiative, has fostered a culture of transparency and collaboration that has accelerated the pace of AI research worldwide. int binary_search(const int *a, int n, int key)
{
    if (n <= 0 || a == NULL) return -1;

    int low = 0;
    int high = n - 1;

    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == key)
            return mid;
        else if (a[mid] < key)
            low = mid + 1;
        else
            high = mid - 1;
    }

    return -1;
}

/* Count the number of set bits (population count) in an unsigned integer. */
static inline unsigned popcount(unsigned x)
{
    /* SWAR (SIMD Within A Register) algorithm – works on any 32‑bit unsigned int. */
    x -= (x >> 1) & 0x55555555u;          /* put count of each 2 bits into each 2‑bit field */
    x = (x & 0x33333333u) + ((x >> 2) & 0x33333333u);  /* sum pairs of 2‑bit fields into 4‑bit fields */

    return (x * 0x01010101u) >> 24;       /* sum the 8‑bit fields into the high byte */
}

void trim(char *s)
{
    if (!s) return;

    /* Skip leading whitespace */
    char *start = s;
    while (*start && (*start == ' ' || *start == '\t' || *start == '\n'))
        ++start;

    /* If the string is all whitespace, make it empty */
    if (*start == '\0') {
        *s = '\0';
        return;
    }

    /* Find the end of the string */
    char *end = start;
    while (*end != '\0')
        ++end;

    /* Skip trailing whitespace */
    while (end > start && (*(end - 1) == ' ' || *(end - 1) == '\t' || *(end - 1) == '\n'))

    /* Move the trimmed string to the beginning */
    size_t len = end - start;          /* length of the trimmed string */
    if (start != s)                    /* shift only if needed */
        memmove(s, start, len + 1);    /* +1 to copy the terminating '\0' */
}

    all_nodes = set(deps.keys())
    for deps_list in deps.values():
        all_nodes.update(deps_list)

    # Build adjacency list: node -> list of dependencies
    adj = {node: deps.get(node, []) for node in all_nodes}

    # Visitation states: 0 = unvisited, 1 = visiting, 2 = visited
    state = {node: 0 for node in all_nodes}
    order = []

    def dfs(node):
        if state[node] == 1:          # cycle detected
            return False
        if state[node] == 2:          # already processed
            return True
        state[node] = 1
        for dep in adj.get(node, []):
            if not dfs(dep):
                return False
        state[node] = 2
        order.append(node)
        return True

    for node in all_nodes:
        if state[node] == 0:
            if not dfs(node):
                return None

    return order[::-1]  # reverse to get dependencies before dependents

- **NFS with TLS support (RHEL 10.0)**  
  *What changed:* NFS now supports Transport Layer Security (TLS) for RPC traffic via kernel TLS (kTLS).  
  *Why it matters:* Encrypts all NFS client‑server communication, protecting data confidentiality and integrity over the network. While the feature is primarily security‑oriented, it also enables compliance with environments that require encrypted NFS traffic, potentially reducing the risk of man‑in‑the‑middle attacks that could otherwise degrade performance.

- **ReaR IPv6 URL parsing bug fix (RHEL 10.0)**  
  *What changed:* ReaR now correctly ignores square brackets in `sshfs://` and `nfs://` URLs containing IPv6 addresses, eliminating the “Invalid scheme ''” error.  
  *Why it matters:* Users can now specify IPv6 NFS endpoints in backup or output URLs without workarounds, preventing abrupt aborts and ensuring reliable use of NFS mounts in backup workflows.

- **Client‑side caching of NFS content via FS‑Cache (RHEL 10.0)**  
  *What changed:* RHEL 10 introduces FS‑Cache integration for NFS, enabling the `cachefiles` back‑end (XFS, ext3, ext4) and the `cachefilesd` daemon to cache NFS data locally.  
  *Why it matters:* Local caching reduces round‑trips to the NFS server, significantly improving read performance and decreasing network bandwidth usage. It also lowers server load, leading to better scalability for workloads with repeated file accesses.

- **NFS with TLS support** – RHEL 10 now supports Transport Layer Security for NFS RPC traffic using kernel TLS.  This adds end‑to‑end encryption for NFS clients and servers, improving security; the encryption overhead can affect throughput and latency, so admins may need to tune for their workload.

- **ReaR nfs:// URL parsing bug fix** – ReaR now correctly interprets IPv6 addresses enclosed in square brackets in `nfs://` (and `sshfs://`) URLs.  This resolves the earlier failure to mount IPv6 NFS shares from backup scripts, improving reliability for IPv6‑only environments.

- **Maximum rsize/wsize for NFS mounts** – The default maximum buffer size for NFS read/write operations is now 1 048 576 bytes (1 MiB).  When `rsize`/`wsize` are not explicitly set, the client/server will negotiate this larger value, yielding higher transfer rates and lower request count compared to earlier smaller defaults.

- **Client‑side FS‑Cache for NFS** – RHEL 10 introduces FS‑Cache support for NFS, enabling a local block‑based cache (XFS/ext3/ext4) via the `cachefiles` backend.  Cached reads/writes are served locally, reducing network traffic and server load, at the cost of some client‑side latency; administrators can enable it to boost performance on high‑traffic NFS workloads.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology, commonly known as MIT, has been a cornerstone of scientific and technological advancement since its founding in 1861, and its influence on the development of artificial intelligence is both profound and multifaceted—spanning foundational theoretical work, pioneering engineering feats, institutional innovation, and the cultivation of generations of AI leaders who have disseminated MIT’s ethos of rigorous inquiry and practical impact across academia, industry, and government laboratories worldwide. From the earliest days of computing, when MIT researchers like Norbert Wiener laid the groundwork for cybernetics—the study of control and communication in animals and machines—MIT established itself as a crucible for ideas that would later crystallize into modern AI. Wiener’s 1948 book *Cybernetics* introduced concepts such as feedback loops and adaptive systems, which became essential to the design of early learning algorithms and robotic control systems. In the mid-1950s, shortly after the term “artificial intelligence” was coined at the Dartmouth Workshop, MIT became one of the first institutions to formally embrace AI as a distinct field of study, establishing the Artificial Intelligence Project in 1959, which would later evolve into the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (AI Lab) in 1966—renamed the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) in 2003 following a merger with the Laboratory for Computer Science. Under the leadership of visionaries like Marvin Minsky, who co-founded the AI Lab and served as its guiding intellectual force for decades, MIT fostered an environment where bold speculation and meticulous experimentation coexisted, producing breakthroughs that shaped the trajectory of AI research. Minsky’s work on neural networks, symbolic reasoning, and the theory of frames—alongside his advocacy for the idea that intelligence emerges from the interaction of simple, specialized agents—challenged prevailing paradigms and inspired decades of research into hybrid architectures that combine connectionist and symbolic approaches. His 1961 paper *Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence* remains a seminal text, outlining a taxonomy of problem-solving strategies and emphasizing the importance of representation, context, and heuristic search—principles that continue to inform AI design today.

The MIT AI Lab was not merely a research center but a cultural phenomenon, attracting brilliant minds from across the globe and cultivating a distinctive “hacker ethic” that prized curiosity, open collaboration, and hands-on tinkering—values that would later permeate the broader software and AI communities. Early projects at the lab included Shakey the Robot, developed in collaboration with SRI International, which became the first general-purpose mobile robot capable of reasoning about its own actions; the development of LISP, a programming language designed specifically for AI research by MIT alumnus John McCarthy (who later moved to Stanford but maintained strong ties to MIT), which became the lingua franca of AI for decades; and the creation of the MIT AI Memo series, an informal yet rigorously peer-reviewed archive of technical reports that served as a vital conduit for disseminating cutting-edge ideas before formal journal publication became common in the field. Among the most influential early outputs was the 1966 Memo 370 by Joseph Weizenbaum, describing ELIZA, one of the first natural language processing programs, which, though intentionally simplistic, sparked widespread public and academic fascination with machine conversation and raised early ethical questions about deception, agency, and human-machine interaction—issues that remain central to AI ethics today. The lab also produced the first computerized chess programs, early expert systems, and foundational work in computer vision, speech recognition, and machine learning, often leveraging MIT’s close ties with the military-industrial complex during the Cold War—particularly through the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)—which provided critical funding for high-risk, high-reward projects that private industry deemed too speculative.

As AI evolved through periods of boom and bust—the infamous “AI winters”—MIT remained a steadfast anchor, adapting its research agenda while preserving its core commitment to scientific integrity and long-term vision. In the 1980s and 1990s, as neural networks fell out of favor due to computational limitations and theoretical challenges, researchers like Tomaso Poggio and Seth Seidman continued to explore biologically inspired models of vision and learning, laying the groundwork for the deep learning revolution that would emerge two decades later. Poggio’s work on regularization, generalization, and the mathematical theory of overparameterized models helped bridge the gap between classical statistics and modern deep learning, while his leadership in establishing MIT’s Center for Brains, Minds and Machines (CBMM)—a multi-institutional NSF Science and Technology Center headquartered at MIT—fostered unprecedented interdisciplinary collaboration between neuroscientists, computer scientists, linguists, and philosophers to understand intelligence in all its forms. CBMM’s research on deep neural networks as models of the visual cortex, for instance, provided empirical and theoretical support for the idea that hierarchical processing in the brain mirrors the architecture of convolutional neural networks, thereby strengthening the scientific plausibility of deep learning approaches and accelerating their adoption in both academia and industry.

The rise of big data and increased computational power in the 2000s and 2010s coincided with a renaissance of AI at MIT, marked by the emergence of new centers and initiatives designed to capitalize on emerging opportunities. The creation of the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) in 2015 reflected a growing recognition that AI’s societal implications were as important as its technical capabilities, and the institute has since become a leader in studying the ethical, economic, and political dimensions of algorithmic decision-making. Simultaneously, the rise of machine learning as a dominant paradigm saw MIT faculty such as Regina Barzilay, who pioneered the application of deep learning to drug discovery and natural language processing—particularly in the domain of biomedical text—and whose work on adversarial robustness and fairness in machine learning has helped define the field’s current ethical standards. Another towering figure is Daniel Jackson, whose contributions to formal methods and software verification have ensured that as AI systems grow more autonomous and complex, they remain reliable, auditable, and trustworthy—a crucial concern in high-stakes domains like healthcare and autonomous vehicles. The work of Daniela Rus, former director of CSAIL and now the Andrew and Erna Vacci Professor at MIT, has been instrumental in advancing robotics and distributed AI systems, including the development of programmable matter and swarm robotics—technologies that promise to transform manufacturing, disaster response, and space exploration.

MIT’s influence extends beyond individual researchers to its institutional architecture and educational philosophy. The Institute has long emphasized the integration of theory and practice, encouraging students to engage in real-world problem-solving through initiatives like the MIT AI Initiative, launched in 2018, which unifies over 1,000 faculty members across 25 departments working on AI-related research. This initiative has catalyzed the creation of new courses, interdisciplinary labs, and industry partnerships, including the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab, established in 2017, which has funded over 100 collaborative projects and produced influential research on large language models, causal inference, and AI for science. MIT’s commitment to open science is also evident in its policy of making research outputs freely available, its support for open-source AI frameworks, and its leadership in initiatives like the AI Ethics and Governance Project, which brings together scholars from law, philosophy, and computer science to develop practical frameworks for responsible AI deployment. Graduates of MIT’s AI programs— numbering in the thousands—have gone on to lead AI research at Google, Facebook (Meta), DeepMind, OpenAI, and countless startups, carrying forward the MIT tradition of bold, principled innovation. Notable alumni include Fei-Fei Li, who co-founded the Stanford AI Lab and was instrumental in the creation of ImageNet, a dataset that revolutionized computer vision; and Rajeev Motwani, whose work on randomized algorithms helped lay the mathematical foundations for modern machine learning.

Perhaps most significantly, MIT has cultivated a culture in which AI is not pursued in isolation but as part of a broader mission to improve human welfare and address global challenges. From climate modeling and pandemic forecasting to personalized education and assistive technologies for people with disabilities, MIT researchers have applied AI to some of humanity’s most pressing problems, often in partnership with NGOs, governments, and international agencies. The work of Dina Katabi and her team at the CSAIL Wireless Center, for instance, has led to the development of RF-Pose, a system that uses radio waves to track human movement through walls—a breakthrough with profound implications for healthcare monitoring and emergency response. Similarly, the development of low-cost, AI-powered diagnostic tools for diseases like malaria and diabetic retinopathy in resource-limited settings exemplifies MIT’s dedication to equitable technological advancement. This mission-driven orientation has also shaped MIT’s approach to AI education, with courses like *6.034 (Introduction to Artificial Intelligence)* and *6.S081 (Special Subject: AI)* emphasizing not only technical proficiency but also critical thinking about the societal consequences of AI. The Institute’s annual AI Week, which features talks, workshops, and demos from leading researchers and practitioners, serves as a living laboratory where students, faculty, and industry leaders converge to debate the future of intelligence—both artificial and human.

In sum, MIT’s influence on AI research is not merely a matter of specific discoveries or famous names, but a deep, systemic imprint on how AI is conceived, developed, and governed. Its legacy is visible in the very architecture of modern AI research—interdisciplinary, ethically conscious, and relentlessly experimental—and in the countless institutions and individuals who trace their intellectual lineage back to the early days of the AI Lab. void reverse_string(char *s) {
    if (s == NULL) return;
    size_t len = 0;
    while (s[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    if (len <= 1) return;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < len / 2; i++) {
        char temp = s[i];
        s[i] = s[len - 1 - i];
        s[len - 1 - i] = temp;
    }
}

#include <ctype.h>

int atoi_strict(const char *s, int *out) {
    if (!s || !out) return -1;
    
    const char *p = s;
    int sign = 1;
    
    // Skip leading whitespace
    while (*p && isspace((unsigned char)*p)) {
        p++;
    }
    
    // Check for sign
    if (*p == '-') {
        sign = -1;
        p++;
    } else if (*p == '+') {
        p++;
    }
    
    // Must have at least one digit
    if (!*p || !isdigit((unsigned char)*p)) {
        return -1;
    }
    
    int value = 0;
    
    // Parse digits
    while (isdigit((unsigned char)*p)) {
        value = value * 10 + (*p - '0');
        p++;
    }
    
    // Skip trailing whitespace
    while (*p && isspace((unsigned char)*p)) {
        p++;
    }
    
    // Must be at end of string
    if (*p != '\0') {
        return -1;
    }
    
    *out = sign * value;
    return 0;
}

import csv

def csv_column_sum(path, col):
    total = 0.0
    with open(path, 'r', newline='') as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        next(reader)  # Skip header row
        for row in reader:
            if col < len(row):
                try:
                    total += float(row[col])
                except (ValueError, IndexError):
                    pass  # Skip non-numeric or missing values
    return total

#include <ctype.h>

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    if (!*pat) {
        return !*str;
    }
    
    if (*pat == '*') {
        // Skip consecutive '*' characters
        while (*pat == '*') {
            pat++;
        }
        
        // Try matching empty string
        if (!*pat) {
            return !*str;
        }
        
        // Try matching with '*' consuming 0 or more characters
        do {
            if (glob_match(pat, str)) {
                return 1;
            }
            if (!*str) {
                break;
            }
            str++;
        } while (1);
        
        return 0;
    }
    
    if (!*str) {
        return 0;
    }
    
    if (*pat == '?') {
        return glob_match(pat + 1, str + 1);
    }
    
    if (*pat != *str) {
        return 0;
    }
    
    return glob_match(pat + 1, str + 1);
}

#include <stddef.h>
#include <string.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    if (line == NULL || out == NULL || cap == 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    const char *p = line;
    int field_num = 0;
    int in_quotes = 0;
    size_t out_pos = 0;

    while (*p != '\0' && field_num <= idx) {
        if (field_num == idx) {
            // Extract current field
            if (out_pos < cap - 1) {
                out[out_pos] = '\0';
            }
            return (int)out_pos;
        }

        if (*p == '"') {
            if (in_quotes) {
                if (p[1] == '"') {
                    // Escaped quote
                    if (out_pos < cap - 1) {
                        out[out_pos++] = '"';
                    }
                    p += 2;
                } else {
                    // End of quoted field
                    in_quotes = 0;
                    p++;
                }
            } else {
                // Start of quoted field
                in_quotes = 1;
                p++;
            }
        } else if (*p == ',' && !in_quotes) {
            // Field separator
            field_num++;
            p++;
        } else {
            // Regular character
            if (out_pos < cap - 1) {
                out[out_pos++] = *p;
            }
            p++;
        }
    }

    // Check if we reached the end of line with the target field
    if (field_num == idx) {
        if (out_pos < cap - 1) {
            out[out_pos] = '\0';
        }
        return (int)out_pos;
    }

    return -1;
}

#include <string.h>
#include <stddef.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    if (line == NULL || out == NULL || cap == 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    const char *p = line;
    int field = 0;

    while (field < idx) {
        // Skip to end of current field
        if (*p == '"') {
            // Quoted field: scan until closing quote
            p++; // skip opening quote
            while (*p != '\0' && *p != '"') {
                if (*p == '"' && *(p + 1) == '"') {
                    p += 2; // skip doubled quote
                } else {
                    p++;
                }
            }
            if (*p == '"') {
                p++; // skip closing quote
            }
        } else {
            // Unquoted field: scan until comma or newline or end
            while (*p != '\0' && *p != ',' && *p != '\r' && *p != '\n') {
                p++;
            }
        }

        if (*p == '\0') {
            return -1; // idx out of range
        }

        // Move past comma
        if (*p == ',') {
            p++;
        }
        field++;
    }

    // Now p points to start of target field
    size_t len = 0;
    if (*p == '"') {
        // Quoted field
        p++; // skip opening quote
        while (*p != '\0' && *p != '"') {
            if (*p == '"' && *(p + 1) == '"') {
                if (len + 1 < cap) {
                    out[len] = '"';
                }
                len++;
                p += 2;
            } else {
                if (len + 1 < cap) {
                    out[len] = *p;
                }
                len++;
                p++;
            }
        }
        if (*p == '"') {
            p++; // skip closing quote
        }
    } else {
        // Unquoted field
        while (*p != '\0' && *p != ',' && *p != '\r' && *p != '\n') {
            if (len + 1 < cap) {
                out[len] = *p;
            }
            len++;
            p++;
        }
    }

    // Null-terminate
    if (len < cap) {
        out[len] = '\0';
    } else {
        out[cap - 1] = '\0';
    }

    return (int)len;
}

    def _diff(path, x, y):
        # If both are dicts, recurse into keys
        if isinstance(x, dict) and isinstance(y, dict):
            result = []
            all_keys = set(x.keys()) | set(y.keys())
            for key in all_keys:
                if key in x and key in y:
                    result.extend(_diff(f"{path}.{key}" if path else key, x[key], y[key]))
                elif key in x:
                    result.append(f"{path}.{key}" if path else key)
                else:
                    result.append(f"{path}.{key}" if path else key)
            return result
        
        # If both are lists, compare by index
        if isinstance(x, list) and isinstance(y, list):
            result = []
            max_len = max(len(x), len(y))
            for i in range(max_len):
                idx_path = f"{path}.{i}" if path else str(i)
                if i < len(x) and i < len(y):
                    result.extend(_diff(idx_path, x[i], y[i]))
                elif i < len(x):
                    result.append(idx_path)
                else:
                    result.append(idx_path)
            return result
        
        # For scalars or mismatched types, compare directly
        if x != y:
            return [path] if path else []
        return []
    
    result = _diff("", a, b)

find_dupes() {
    local dir="$1"
    if [[ -z "$dir" || ! -d "$dir" ]]; then
        echo "Usage: find_dupes <dir>" >&2
        return 1
    fi

    # Create temp file for hash-path pairs
    local tmpfile
    tmpfile=$(mktemp)
    trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT

    # Find all regular files and compute MD5 hashes
    # Use md5 -r for BSD/macOS compatibility
    find "$dir" -type f -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
        hash=$(md5 -r "$file" | awk '{print $1}')
        printf '%s\t%s\n' "$hash" "$file"
    done > "$tmpfile"

    # Sort by hash, then by path, and group duplicates
    sort -t $'\t' -k1,1 -k2,2 "$tmpfile" | awk -F'\t' '

        if ($1 == prev_hash) {
            paths[NR] = $2
            count++
        } else {
            if (count > 1) {
                # Sort the collected paths for this group

            for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
                printf "%s%s", sorted_paths[i], (i < n ? " " : "\n")
            }
        }
    }' | sort
}

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, commonly known as MIT, stands as a colossal monolith in the landscape of modern scientific and technological advancement, a status that is particularly pronounced and profound within the specific domain of artificial intelligence, where the institution has not merely participated in the evolution of the field but has actively shaped its trajectory, defining its theoretical underpinnings, its ethical frameworks, and its practical applications in ways that have rippled outward to influence global research paradigms, industrial practices, and societal expectations. To understand the magnitude of MIT’s influence on AI, one must first look back to the mid-twentieth century, specifically to the seminal Dartmouth Conference of 1956, which is widely regarded as the birth of AI as a distinct academic discipline, a gathering that was heavily influenced by the intellectual currents flowing through Cambridge, Massachusetts, and where key figures who would later become central to MIT’s AI narrative were either present or deeply connected to the emerging community, establishing a foundational ethos that viewed intelligence not as a mystical property but as a computational process that could be modeled, analyzed, and eventually replicated by machines. This early commitment to the computational theory of mind laid the groundwork for the establishment of the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1959, a move that was revolutionary in its time because it was one of the first instances of a major university dedicating a specific, well-funded laboratory to the study of machine intelligence, signaling to the world that AI was not a fringe curiosity but a serious area of scientific inquiry worthy of institutional support and rigorous academic scrutiny. The AI Lab, under the leadership of pioneers such as John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, and Seymour Papert, became a crucible for innovation, producing seminal works that defined the early landscape of the field, including the development of the LISP programming language, which became the dominant language for AI research for decades due to its suitability for symbolic manipulation and its functional programming features that aligned well with the logic-based approaches prevalent at the time. Minsky, in particular, emerged as a towering figure whose work on the nature of intelligence, perception, and the architecture of the mind provided a theoretical backbone for the field, arguing that intelligence is the ability to achieve goals in a complex environment and that this could be achieved through the interaction of simple, specialized processes, a perspective that influenced generations of researchers who sought to build systems that could reason, plan, and learn. However, the influence of MIT on AI was not limited to the symbolic, logic-based approaches of the early years; the institution also played a pivotal role in the development of connectionist models and neural networks, a shift that was catalyzed by the work of researchers who recognized the limitations of purely symbolic systems and sought to model the brain’s parallel processing capabilities. The resurgence of interest in neural networks in the 1980s and 1990s, often referred to as the "neural net" era, saw MIT researchers contributing to the development of backpropagation algorithms and the application of these models to pattern recognition tasks, laying the groundwork for the deep learning revolution that would explode in the 21st century. This transition from symbolic AI to sub-symbolic, data-driven approaches was not a clean break but a complex interplay of ideas, and MIT’s strength lay in its ability to foster this diversity of thought, allowing researchers to explore multiple paradigms simultaneously and to draw connections between seemingly disparate fields such as computer science, cognitive science, neuroscience, and mathematics. The establishment of the MIT Media Lab in 1985 by Nicholas Negroponte further expanded the scope of MIT’s influence on AI by introducing a new philosophy of research that emphasized the integration of technology with human experience, art, and society, moving away from the purely technical focus of the AI Lab and towards a more holistic view of how intelligent systems could interact with people and environments. The Media Lab’s interdisciplinary approach encouraged the development of AI applications in areas such as robotics, human-computer interaction, and creative technologies, leading to breakthroughs in fields like gesture recognition, natural language processing, and autonomous systems, and fostering a culture of innovation that valued practical impact and user-centered design. This emphasis on the human element of AI was a distinctive feature of MIT’s contribution, as it recognized that the ultimate goal of AI was not just to create machines that could think, but to create systems that could enhance human capabilities and improve quality of life, a perspective that has become increasingly important as AI systems have become more pervasive in daily life. In the modern era, MIT’s influence on AI has been further amplified by its leadership in the development of deep learning and machine learning techniques, with researchers at the institution making significant contributions to the understanding of how neural networks learn, how they can be made more efficient, and how they can be applied to a wide range of complex problems. The work of MIT researchers in areas such as computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning has been instrumental in advancing the state of the art, with many of the foundational algorithms and architectures that are now standard in the field having their roots in research conducted at MIT or by alumni who were trained there. For example, the development of convolutional neural networks for image recognition, a technique that has revolutionized fields from medical imaging to autonomous driving, has been significantly advanced by MIT researchers who have explored new ways to train and optimize these models, making them more accurate and robust. Similarly, in the area of natural language processing, MIT has been at the forefront of the shift from rule-based systems to statistical and neural approaches, contributing to the development of large language models that can understand and generate human-like text, a development that has profound implications for communication, education, and information access. Beyond the technical contributions, MIT has also played a crucial role in shaping the ethical and social discourse surrounding AI, recognizing that the development of powerful intelligent systems carries significant risks and responsibilities. The institution has been a leader in the field of AI ethics, with researchers and faculty members actively engaging in discussions about bias, fairness, transparency, and accountability in AI systems, advocating for the development of AI that is not only powerful but also just and beneficial to society. This ethical focus is reflected in the curriculum, with courses that integrate technical training with discussions of the social implications of AI, and in the research agenda, with projects that aim to mitigate the negative impacts of AI and to ensure that its benefits are shared broadly. The MIT Media Lab, in particular, has been a hub for this kind of socially conscious research, exploring how AI can be used to address social challenges such as inequality, access to education, and environmental sustainability. This holistic approach to AI, which combines technical excellence with ethical responsibility and social awareness, has set a standard for other institutions and has influenced the way that AI is taught, researched, and deployed around the world. Furthermore, MIT’s influence extends beyond its own campus and into the broader ecosystem of AI research and industry, through the training of generations of researchers, engineers, and entrepreneurs who have gone on to lead major AI initiatives at universities, research labs, and companies around the globe. The MIT alumni network is a powerful force in the AI world, with many prominent figures in the field having been educated or trained at the institution, creating a community of practice that shares common values, methodologies, and perspectives. This network effect has amplified MIT’s impact, as ideas and innovations developed at MIT have been disseminated and adapted by its alumni, contributing to the global advancement of AI. The institution’s strong ties to industry, through partnerships, consulting, and the founding of spin-off companies, have also ensured that its research has practical applications and that its innovations are translated into real-world products and services, further cementing its role as a leader in the field. In conclusion, the influence of MIT on artificial intelligence is vast, multifaceted, and enduring, spanning from the foundational theoretical work of the mid-twentieth century to the cutting-edge research of the twenty-first century, and encompassing technical, ethical, and social dimensions. By establishing the first dedicated AI laboratory, fostering a culture of interdisciplinary innovation, leading the way in the development of deep learning and machine learning, and championing the ethical and social implications of AI, MIT has not only contributed to the advancement of the field but has also shaped its identity and its future direction. Its legacy is one of intellectual rigor, creative vision, and a commitment to using technology for the betterment of humanity, a legacy that continues to inspire and guide researchers and practitioners around the world as they navigate the complex and rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence. The story of MIT and AI is a testament to the power of sustained institutional commitment, the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration, and the profound impact that a single institution can have on the trajectory of a transformative technology, ensuring that MIT remains a central pillar in the ongoing narrative of machine intelligence and its role in shaping our future.

void trim(char *s) {
    if (s == NULL) return;

    /* Strip leading whitespace */
    while (*s == ' ' || *s == '\t' || *s == '\n') {
        s++;
    }

    /* If the string is now empty, we're done */
    if (*s == '\0') return;

    /* Find the end of the string */
    char *end = s;
    while (*end != '\0') {
        end++;
    }
    end--; /* points to last character */

    /* Strip trailing whitespace */
    while (end >= s && (*end == ' ' || *end == '\t' || *end == '\n')) {
        *end = '\0';
        end--;
    }
}

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    const char *p = pat;
    const char *s = str;
    const char *star_p = NULL;
    const char *star_s = NULL;

    while (*s) {
        if (*p == '*') {
            star_p = p++;
            star_s = s;
            while (*star_p == '*') star_p++;
        } else if (*p == '?' || *p == *s) {

            p = star_p + 1;
            s = ++star_s;

            return 0;

    return *p == '\0' ? 1 : 0;
}

#include <stddef.h>

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap) {
    if (line == NULL || out == NULL || cap == 0) {
        return -1;
    }

    const char *p = line;
    int field_idx = 0;

    for (;;) {
        /* Skip leading whitespace? RFC 4180 doesn't specify, but typically no.
           We just start parsing the field. */
        
        int in_quotes = 0;
        size_t out_len = 0;
        
        if (*p == '"') {
            in_quotes = 1;
            p++;
        }
        
        while (*p != '\0') {
            if (in_quotes) {
                if (*p == '"') {
                    if (*(p + 1) == '"') {
                        /* Escaped quote */
                        if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                            out[out_len++] = '"';
                        }
                        p += 2;
                    } else {
                        /* End of quoted field */
                        p++;
                        break;
                    }
                } else {
                    if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                        out[out_len++] = *p;
                    }
                    p++;
                }
            } else {
                if (*p == ',') {
                    p++;
                    break;
                } else if (*p == '\0') {
                    break;
                } else {
                    if (out_len < cap - 1) {
                        out[out_len++] = *p;
                    }
                    p++;
                }
            }
        }
        
        /* NUL terminate */
        out[out_len] = '\0';
        
        if (field_idx == idx) {
            return (int)out_len;
        }
        
        /* Move to next field */
        if (*p == '\0') {
            /* End of line, no more fields */
            return -1;
        }
        
        /* p should be at ',' or '\0' */
        if (*p == ',') {
            p++;
            field_idx++;
        } else {
            /* Unexpected state, but treat as end */
            return -1;
        }
    }
}

int csv_field(const char *line, int idx, char *out, size_t cap)
{
    if (cap == 0)
        return -1;

    const char *p = line;
    int field_idx = 0;

    for (;;) {
        /* Skip to the start of the current field */
        int quoted = 0;
        if (*p == '"') {
            quoted = 1;
            p++;
        }

        size_t out_len = 0;
        int in_quotes = quoted;

        while (*p) {
            if (in_quotes) {
                if (*p == '"') {
                    if (p[1] == '"') {
                        /* doubled quote -> single quote */
                        if (out_len < cap - 1)
                            out[out_len++] = '"';
                        p += 2;
                    } else {
                        /* closing quote */
                        in_quotes = 0;
                        p++;
                        /* After closing quote, the next char should be ',' or '\0' or '\r' */
                        if (*p == '\r') {
                            p++;
                        }
                        if (*p == ',') {
                            p++;
                            break;
                        } else if (*p == '\0') {
                            break;
                        } else {
                            /* Malformed: non-comma, non-NUL after closing quote.
                               Per RFC 4180 this is invalid, but we'll treat the rest
                               as literal until next comma or end. */
                            /* Continue parsing as unquoted */
                            in_quotes = 0;
                            /* don't consume the unexpected char; fall through to unquoted handling */
                            goto unquoted;
                        }
                    }
                } else {
                    if (out_len < cap - 1)
                        out[out_len++] = *p;
                    p++;
                }
            } else {
                if (*p == ',') {
                    p++;
                    break;
                } else if (*p == '\0') {
                    break;
                } else if (*p == '\r') {
                    p++;
                    if (*p == '\n')
                        p++;
                    break;
                } else {
unquoted:
                    if (out_len < cap - 1)
                        out[out_len++] = *p;
                    p++;
                }
            }
        }

        /* If we reached end of line, this is the last field */
        if (*p == '\0') {
            out[out_len] = '\0';
            return (int)out_len;
        }

        /* We consumed a comma; move to next field */
        field_idx++;
        if (field_idx == idx) {
            out[out_len] = '\0';
            return (int)out_len;
        }
        if (field_idx > idx) {
            break;
        }
    }

    return -1;
}

find_dupes() {
    local dir="$1"
    local -a files=()
    local -A md5_to_files=()

    # Find all regular files recursively
    while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
        files+=("$file")
    done < <(find "$dir" -type f -print0)

    # Compute MD5 for each file and group by hash
    local file md5
    for file in "${files[@]}"; do
        md5=$(md5 -r "$file" | awk '{print $1}')
        if [[ -n "${md5_to_files[$md5]+x}" ]]; then
            md5_to_files[$md5]+=" $file"
        else
            md5_to_files[$md5]="$file"
        fi
    done

    # Collect groups with 2+ files
    local -a groups=()
    local group
    for group in "${md5_to_files[@]}"; do
        # Count files in this group
        local -a group_files=($group)
        if (( ${#group_files[@]} >= 2 )); then
            # Sort the files in this group
            local sorted_group
            sorted_group=$(printf '%s\n' "${group_files[@]}" | sort)
            groups+=("$sorted_group")
        fi
    done

    # Sort groups by their first path
    if (( ${#groups[@]} > 0 )); then
        printf '%s\n' "${groups[@]}" | sort -k1,1
    fi
}

    done < <(find "$dir" -type f -print0)

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) stands as a global epicenter of intellectual rigor, a crucible where the boundaries of human understanding are constantly pushed, redefined, and shattered, particularly within the rapidly evolving domain of artificial intelligence. To understand the profound influence of MIT on AI research is to trace the history of modern computation itself, as the institution has functioned not merely as a school, but as a foundational architect of the digital age. The relationship between MIT and AI is symbiotic; the university provides the theoretical frameworks and the experimental playgrounds, while the global technological landscape provides the real-world complexity that validates and drives these academic pursuits. At the heart of this influence is a unique ecosystem that blends deep mathematical theory with an aggressive, hands-on engineering culture. This dual focus ensures that research at MIT is never purely abstract; it is always oriented toward the realization of physical or computational systems that can interact with the world. The history of AI at MIT is marked by a lineage of thinkers who transitioned from the early days of symbolic logic and heuristic-based programming to the modern era of massive neural networks and deep learning. This progression was not linear but was instead characterized by periods of intense breakthrough followed by periods of refinement, with MIT often serving as the catalyst for the shifts in paradigm. The influence of the institution is felt through its faculty, its research labs, such as the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), and its vast network of alumni who lead the world’s most significant technology firms.

The Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) serves as the nerve center for much of this activity, acting as a microcosm of the broader AI revolution. Within its walls, researchers engage in a multidisciplinary approach that recognizes AI is not just a subset of computer science, but a convergence of mathematics, cognitive science, robotics, linguistics, and philosophy. This interdisciplinary nature is critical because the challenges of AI—such as achieving general intelligence, ensuring robustness, and understanding the mechanics of learning—cannot be solved through a single lens. At CSAIL, the focus often oscillates between the "top-down" approach of symbolic AI, which seeks to encode human-like reasoning through logic, and the "bottom-up" approach of connectionism, which seeks to mimic the biological structures of the brain. This tension has historically driven much of the progress in the field, as researchers at MIT have been at the forefront of both the classical AI era and the modern statistical learning revolution. The ability to bridge these two worlds—to understand how a machine might reason logically while also learning through pattern recognition—is one of the primary intellectual contributions of the MIT community. Furthermore, the institution’s emphasis on hardware-software co-design has been instrumental in the development of AI. While much of the world focuses on the algorithms, MIT researchers have long understood that the efficiency of an AI model is inextricably linked to the architecture of the silicon it runs on. This understanding has led to breakthroughs in neuromorphic computing and specialized AI accelerators, ensuring that the theoretical leaps in machine learning are matched by the physical capacity to execute them at scale.

The influence of MIT extends far beyond the theoretical; it is deeply embedded in the practical application of AI to solve the most pressing problems of humanity. The university’s commitment to "mens et manu"—mind and hand—means that AI research is frequently applied to robotics, biotechnology, and climate modeling. In the realm of robotics, MIT has been a pioneer in creating autonomous systems that can navigate the messy, unpredictable environments of the real world. The work done in the laboratory on legged locomotion, tactile sensing, and human-robot interaction has laid the groundwork for the next generation of autonomous vehicles and service robots. These are not merely academic exercises; they are attempts to translate the abstract concept of "intelligence" into physical agency. Similarly, the intersection of AI and biology at MIT has opened new frontiers in protein folding, drug discovery, and genomic analysis. By applying deep learning models to the complexities of biological systems, researchers are essentially treating the code of life as a computational problem, leading to discoveries that were previously thought to be decades away. This application-driven research serves as a feedback loop: the complexities of real-world data force researchers to develop more sophisticated models, which in turn lead to even more profound discoveries. This cycle of constant refinement is what keeps MIT at the vanguard of the field.

Moreover, the ethical and philosophical dimensions of AI are central to the discourse at MIT. As AI systems become increasingly integrated into the fabric of society, the questions of bias, transparency, accountability, and safety become existential. MIT has been a leading voice in the critical examination of these issues, fostering a culture where the social implications of technology are studied with the same rigor as the algorithms themselves. The university’s researchers have been instrumental in developing methods for "explainable AI," seeking to peel back the black box of deep learning to understand why a machine makes a specific decision. This work is vital for the deployment of AI in sensitive areas like healthcare, law, and finance, where human trust is a prerequisite for adoption. By centering ethics in the research process, MIT helps shape the global standards for responsible AI development. This is not merely about avoiding harm; it is about proactively designing systems that align with human values. The intellectual leadership provided by MIT in this area ensures that the technological progress of the future is not just rapid, but also directed toward the betterment of the human condition.

The global impact of MIT’s AI research is also seen in the massive talent pipeline it produces. The researchers, PhD students, and undergraduates who pass through the institution become the architects of the global AI economy. When an MIT-trained engineer moves to Silicon Valley or starts a venture-backed startup, they carry with them a specific methodology: a blend of rigorous mathematical skepticism and an optimistic, engineering-driven approach to problem-solving. This "MIT DNA" is visible in the leadership of many of the world's most influential AI companies, where the principles of scalability, efficiency, and radical innovation are prioritized. This creates a global network of influence where the breakthroughs occurring in Cambridge, Massachusetts, ripple through the global economy, affecting everything from how we search for information to how we manage global logistics. The institution’s ability to attract the brightest minds from every corner of the globe ensures that its research is informed by a diversity of perspectives, which is essential for tackling the universal challenges of intelligence.

As we move deeper into the era of artificial intelligence, the role of MIT is expected to evolve but not diminish. The transition from narrow AI to more general, versatile systems will require a fundamental rethinking of many current paradigms. MIT is uniquely positioned to lead this transition because its research is not tethered to the current technological zeitgeist; it is built on the ability to question the very foundations of what we know. Whether it is the development of quantum-enhanced machine learning or the exploration of the intersection between AI and consciousness, the institution remains a place where the impossible is treated as a technical challenge to be solved. The influence of MIT on AI is not just a matter of publishing papers or winning awards; it is about the shaping of the future itself. As AI becomes the primary tool through which humanity interacts with reality, the intellectual frameworks developed at MIT will serve as the scaffolding for the digital civilization of the 21st century and beyond. The institution’s legacy is not just in the machines it helps create, but in the expansion of the human capacity to understand, to reason, and to innovate. Through its relentless pursuit of knowledge and its commitment to the practical application of that knowledge, MIT continues to define the trajectory of artificial intelligence, ensuring that the own intelligence of humanity is augmented by the very tools we create to mimic it. The interplay between the human mind and the machine, facilitated by the rigorous inquiry of MIT, remains one of the most significant intellectual endeavors in human history, a journey that is only just beginning to reach its full potential. In the end, the influence of MIT on AI is a testament to the power of concentrated human intellect when it is directed toward the most profound questions of existence: how do we learn, how do we think, and how do we build a future that reflects our highest aspirations? Through its work, MIT provides the answers, one breakthrough at a time.

csv_col() {
    local target_name="$1"
    local col_idx
    
    # Read header to find column index
    IFS=',' read -r -a header
    for i in "${!header[@]}"; do
        if [[ "${header[$i]}" == "$target_name" ]]; then
            col_idx=$((i + 1))
            break
        fi
    done

    if [[ -z "$col_idx" ]]; then
        return 1
    fi

    # Use awk to handle the extraction

double rpn_eval(const char *expr) {
    double *stack = malloc(strlen(expr) + 1);
    int top = -1;

    char *expr_copy = strdup(expr);
    char *token = strtok(expr_copy, " ");

    while (token != NULL) {
        if (isdigit(token[0])) {
            stack[++top] = atof(token);
        } else {
            double b = stack[top--];
            double a = stack[top--];
            if (token[0] == '+') stack[++top] = a + b;
            else if (token[0] == '-') stack[++top] = a - b;
            else if (token[0] == '*') stack[++top] = a * b;
            else if (token[0] == '/') stack[++top] = a / b;
        }
        token = strtok(NULL, " ");
    }

    double result = stack[0];
    free(stack);
    free(expr_copy);
    return result;
}

* **NFS with TLS support:** Adds support for Transport Layer Security (TLS) via kernel TLS (kTLS). This enhances security by enabling encrypted communication between clients and servers for RPC traffic.
* **ReaR IPv6 bracket fix:** Fixed an issue where square brackets used for IPv6 addresses (e.g., `[::1]`) were incorrectly interpreted as shell metacharacters in `sshfs://` or `nfs://` URLs. This allows for successful automated backups/recovery using IPv6 addresses in `BACKUP_URL` or `OUTPUT_URL`.
* **FS-Cache (Client-side caching):** Provides a mechanism to use local block-based file systems (XFS, ext3, ext4) as a cache back end via the `cachefiles` kernel module and `cachefilesd` daemon. This improves performance and reduces network/server load by satisfying read requests locally.
* **NFS Transfer Sizes:** The maximum `rsize` and `wsize` (read/write size) is set to 1,048,576 bytes in RHEL 10. This allows for larger data transfers per operation compared to older standards.

* **NFS with TLS support:** Adds support for Transport Layer Security (TLS) via kernel TLS (kTLS). This enhances security by enabling encrypted communication between clients and servers for RPC traffic.
* **ReaR IPv6 support fix:** Fixed an issue where square brackets in IPv6 addresses were incorrectly interpreted as shell metacharacters when using `sshfs://` or `nfs://` schemes in `BACKUP_URL` or `OUTPUT_URL`. This allows for successful automated backups using IPv6 addresses in these URLs.
* **NFS client-side caching (FS-Cache):** Introduces/documents the use of `cachefiles` and `cachefilesd` to enable client-side caching of NFS content. This can significantly reduce network bandwidth and server load by satisfying read requests from a local block-based file system (XFS, ext3, or ext4).
* **NFS transfer size limits:** The maximum `rsize` and `wsize` (read/write size) is set to 1,048,576 bytes in RHEL 10. This defines the maximum amount of data transferred in a single operation, impacting throughput and efficiency.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) has long been a cornerstone of artificial intelligence research, shaping the field through groundbreaking discoveries, innovative methodologies, and a culture of interdisciplinary collaboration. Since its inception, MIT has fostered an environment where theoretical computer science, cognitive psychology, engineering, and mathematics converge to push the boundaries of what machines can achieve. The institute’s influence on AI is evident in its foundational contributions to machine learning, robotics, natural language processing, and even the philosophical underpinnings of intelligence itself. From the early days of symbolic AI to the modern era of deep learning, MIT researchers have consistently driven progress, often setting the standard for the entire discipline.

One of MIT’s most enduring legacies in AI stems from its role in the development of symbolic AI, or "Good Old-Fashioned AI" (GOFAI), during the mid-20th century. Pioneers like Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert, co-founders of MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (now the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, or CSAIL), laid the groundwork for rule-based systems that attempted to replicate human reasoning. Minsky’s work on neural networks in the 1950s, though initially overshadowed by the rise of symbolic approaches, later resurfaced as a critical component of modern AI. His book *Perceptrons*, co-authored with Papert, was a seminal text that both critiqued early neural network models and inadvertently spurred research into more robust architectures. The AI Lab at MIT became a hub for exploring how machines could manipulate symbols to solve problems, leading to advancements in theorem proving, expert systems, and even early attempts at natural language understanding.

The influence of MIT’s AI research extended beyond academia into industry and government, particularly during the Cold War era when the U.S. military sought to leverage AI for strategic advantage. Projects like the *Automated Reasoning Project*, funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), aimed to create systems capable of logical deduction and problem-solving. MIT’s involvement in these initiatives not only accelerated technological progress but also established the institute as a key player in shaping national AI policy. The collaboration between MIT researchers and defense contractors fostered a symbiotic relationship that continues today, with MIT’s spin-off companies and startups often emerging from military-funded research.

As the field of AI evolved, MIT adapted its approach, embracing statistical methods and machine learning that would later dominate the landscape. The 1980s and 1990s saw a shift away from purely symbolic systems toward hybrid models that incorporated probability and data-driven learning. Researchers like Tom Mitchell, who later became a professor at Carnegie Mellon but began his career at MIT, contributed to the development of Bayesian networks and other probabilistic frameworks that improved AI’s ability to handle uncertainty. MIT’s Media Lab, founded in 1985 by Nicholas Negroponte, further expanded the scope of AI by exploring its applications in human-computer interaction, affective computing, and even artistic creation. Projects like the *Affective Computing* group, led by Rosalind Picard, pioneered the idea that machines could recognize and respond to human emotions, a concept that is now integral to modern AI systems like virtual assistants and social robots.

The turn of the 21st century marked another pivotal moment for MIT’s influence on AI, as the institute became a driving force behind the resurgence of neural networks and deep learning. Researchers like Yoshua Bengio, who frequently collaborated with MIT faculty, built upon earlier work by Minsky and others to develop deep neural architectures capable of learning hierarchical representations from raw data. MIT’s involvement in this revival was multifaceted, with professors like Tomaso Poggio leading efforts to understand the biological plausibility of deep learning models and their potential for advancing cognitive science. The institute’s *Center for Brains, Minds, and Machines*, a DARPA-funded initiative launched in 2013, brought together neuroscientists, computer scientists, and engineers to explore the intersection of artificial and biological intelligence. This interdisciplinary approach has yielded insights into how the human brain processes information, which in turn informs the design of more efficient and capable AI systems.

MIT’s impact on AI is not limited to theoretical research; the institute has also been a crucible for practical innovations that have transformed industries. The development of the *Lego Mindstorms* platform, for example, emerged from MIT’s work in educational robotics and has since become a staple in STEM education worldwide. Similarly, MIT’s *CSAIL* has produced technologies like the *Kinect* motion-sensing system, which was originally developed for the Xbox gaming console but has since found applications in healthcare, manufacturing, and autonomous vehicles. The institute’s emphasis on real-world impact is evident in its numerous startup companies, many of which have commercialized AI research. Companies like *iRobot*, founded by MIT alumni Colin Angle and Helen Greiner, have brought robotic vacuum cleaners and military drones to market, while *KnuEdge*, co-founded by MIT professor Ramesh Raskar, specializes in AI-driven video analytics for security and surveillance.

Beyond technology, MIT has shaped the ethical and societal discussions surrounding AI. The institute’s *Initiative on the Digital Economy*, launched in 2015, examines the economic and social implications of AI, including its effects on labor markets, privacy, and inequality. Researchers like Ethan Zuckerman explore how AI can amplify or mitigate biases in society, while others, like Cynthia Breazeal, investigate the ethical considerations of human-robot interaction. MIT’s *Media Lab* has also been a vocal advocate for responsible innovation, promoting transparency and accountability in AI development. These efforts reflect the institute’s recognition that AI’s influence extends far beyond technical achievements, encompassing profound questions about autonomy, agency, and the future of human civilization.

The global reach of MIT’s AI research is evident in its collaborations with institutions worldwide. The *MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab*, established in 2017, is a prime example of how MIT leverages industry partnerships to advance AI. This lab focuses on areas like machine learning, quantum computing, and healthcare, with the goal of developing AI systems that can tackle some of society’s most pressing challenges. Similarly, MIT’s *Singapore-ETH Centre* and other international initiatives bring together researchers from different cultural and academic backgrounds to address problems like climate change and urbanization through AI-driven solutions. These collaborations underscore MIT’s role as a global leader in AI, one that transcends geographical boundaries to foster collective progress.

In recent years, MIT has continued to innovate in AI by exploring emerging domains such as explainable AI, federated learning, and edge computing. The *MIT Quest for Intelligence*, launched in 2018, is a university-wide effort to understand the nature of intelligence in both machines and humans. This initiative brings together researchers from diverse fields to investigate questions like how AI can be made more interpretable, how it can operate efficiently on resource-constrained devices, and how it can adapt to dynamic environments. The quest reflects MIT’s commitment to pushing the frontiers of AI while addressing the limitations of current technologies.

The influence of MIT on AI research is also evident in its educational programs, which have produced generations of leaders in the field. The institute’s undergraduate and graduate courses in AI, machine learning, and robotics are among the most rigorous and sought-after in the world. Programs like the *MIT Schwarzman College of Computing*, established in 2018, integrate computing and AI into every discipline at MIT, ensuring that future engineers, scientists, and policymakers are equipped with the skills to harness AI’s potential.         length++;

void trim(char *s) {
    if (!s) return;

    while (isspace((unsigned char)*p)) {
        p++;

#include <ctype.h>

int atoi_strict(const char *s, int *out) {
    const char *p = s;
    int sign = 1;
    long val = 0;

    while (isspace((unsigned char)*p)) {
        p++;
    }

    if (*p == '+') {
        p++;
    } else if (*p == '-') {
        sign = -1;
        p++;
    }

    if (!isdigit((unsigned char)*p)) {
        return -1;
    }

    while (isdigit((unsigned char)*p)) {
        val = val * 10 + (*p - '0');
        p++;
    }

    if (*p != '\0') {
        return -1;
    }

    if (val > INT_MAX) {
        return -1;
    }

    *out = sign * val;
    return 0;
}

#include <stddef.h>

int glob_match(const char *pat, const char *str) {
    while (*pat) {
        if (*pat == '*') {
            if (!*str) return 1;
            for (size_t i = 0; str[i]; i++) {
                if (glob_match(pat + 1, str + i)) return 1;
            }
            return 0;
        } else if (*pat == '?') {
            if (!*str) return 0;
            pat++;
            str++;
        } else {
            if (*pat != *str) return 0;
            pat++;
            str++;
        }
    }
    return !*str;
}
